lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Guided practice: asking for help early and well

objective: Learners practice asking a supervisor for help on a fictional stuck-task scenario, out loud with a trusted adult playing the supervisor, before the moment they actually need this script at a real job, so asking early feels routine rather than like an admission of failure.
scenario: Given a short fictional workplace scenario where the learner is stuck on a task and unsure whether to keep struggling or ask, the learner practices the ask out loud with a trusted adult playing the supervisor, then revises the ask based on feedback.
safetyNotes: No audio or video recording is made; the adult gives live feedback and the learner writes notes afterward.
The practice scenario is fictional and does not require the learner to discuss any real job or real workplace situation.

simulationAlternative.description: If no adult is available to role-play the supervisor, the learner instead writes both sides of the conversation as a short script, then reads only their own side aloud once and self-checks it against the same look-fors.

tasks.directions: Before practicing, write down what makes asking for help at work feel harder than asking a friend.

prompts.text: What is one reason asking a supervisor for help might feel harder than asking a classmate or friend?

tasks.directions: With your adult playing the supervisor, practice asking for help on the fictional stuck-task scenario, saying what you tried and what you're stuck on.

prompts.text: I stated what I had already tried before asking.
I named specifically what I was stuck on, not just 'I don't get it.'
My adult gave specific feedback on the ask.

tasks.directions: Revise your ask based on the feedback and write the improved version.

prompts.text: Write your revised version of asking for help, and explain what you changed.

tasks.directions: Reflect on the timing of asking for help.

prompts.text: In the fictional scenario, at what point should the character have asked for help, and how would you recognize that same point in a real task?

remediation: If the learner's ask omits what they already tried (making it sound like they haven't attempted the task at all), reteach the three-part structure: what I tried, what specifically isn't working, what I need, modeling one complete example before the learner retries their own ask using that structure.
extension: Have the learner practice a second, harder version: asking for help after having made a mistake that needs to be reported, not just a task they're stuck on, using the same three-part structure adapted for admitting an error.
